title: Ulyana and the Extraction
premise: Odile Nystrom, a whistle-blower living under four names, discovers her safe house listed for sale online — complete with interior photos that could only have been taken by someone inside. The listing is a message from Voss, the assassin who has hunted her for three years, and it means her protectors inside a covert EU extraction program have sold her out. To survive, Odile must move the evidence of a tri-government cover-up — a massacre in the Baltic, buried to protect an arms deal — past three governments and one assassin before the sale closes and her location is confirmed. Betrayed by the handler she trusted most, she allies with a disgraced journalist and a rogue archivist, trading her anonymity for justice. In the end, Odile releases the archive publicly at devastating personal cost, confronts Voss not with violence but with the truth of who ordered him, and finally chooses one name — her own.
about_author: Bram Pemberton is the pen name of a former intelligence analyst turned novelist who writes from a coastal town he refuses to name on maps. His thrillers are known for their procedural precision and their obsession with what documents remember that people forget.

chapters.title: The House That Wasn't Empty
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Scrolling property listings out of habit, she finds her safe house photographed from within — her chipped mug on the counter, her coat on the hook. Panic sets in as she realizes someone stood inside and lived. Emotional beat: the floor dropping out of a carefully built invisible life.

chapters.title: Four Names, One Woman
chapters.summary: Odile's POV, flashback-woven. She inventories her identities — bank cards, accents, dead-letter drops — trying to find which one leaked. Each alias carries a scar from a different year of running. Emotional beat: grief for the woman she was before the first name change.

chapters.title: The Handler's Voice
chapters.summary: Odile calls Marek, her extraction-program handler, using a burner. He is calm, too calm, and tells her to stay put — advice that now sounds like a trap. She notices his background noise: an airport. Emotional beat: loyalty curdling into suspicion mid-conversation.

chapters.title: Voss Sends Regards
chapters.summary: Voss's POV. The assassin reviews the listing he commissioned, noting the buyer is fictional and the real purpose is pressure: flush Odile toward her emergency route, which he has mapped. We learn he doesn't hate her; he respects her. Emotional beat: cold professionalism shadowed by something almost like regret.

chapters.title: The Baltic File
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. She reopens the encrypted archive: evidence that a 2019 maritime 'accident' killed eleven civilians to protect an arms corridor, signed off across three governments. The file is why she runs; the file is also her only leverage. Emotional beat: resolve hardening — she stops planning escape and starts planning exposure.

chapters.title: A Journalist With Nothing Left
chapters.summary: Ines Kovač's POV. A disgraced reporter in Riga, ruined for chasing the same massacre, receives a dead-drop note in Odile's handwriting. She knows it's bait or salvation, possibly both. Emotional beat: cynical hope — the addict's pull of one last real story.

chapters.title: The Archivist Who Kept Copies
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. A rogue records clerk in Brussels reveals he duplicated the program's internal logs years ago, including orders tracing to Odile's own handler. He agrees to meet her but insists on conditions. Emotional beat: quiet courage of a bureaucrat who chose memory over career.

chapters.title: Sale Closing in Nine Days
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Decoding the listing's metadata, she finds the closing date — nine days — and understands Voss's timeline is hers now. She maps three routes out of Europe and hates all of them. Emotional beat: claustrophobia; every map looks like a cage.

chapters.title: Marek's Apartment
chapters.summary: Odile breaks into Marek's flat and finds payment records linking him to the listing's shell company — and a child's drawing addressed to 'Uncle M.' from one of the massacre victims' families. Emotional beat: betrayal complicated by pity; she leaves without taking anything but copies.

chapters.title: Train to Gdańsk
chapters.summary: Odile and Ines travel under borrowed papers, testing each other's stories across a dining car table. Ines spots a surveillance tail Odile missed. Emotional beat: two guarded women discovering they work well together — trust as a skill, not a feeling.

chapters.title: What the Harbor Remembers
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. At the massacre site, a retired dockworker gives her a salvaged ship's log contradicting the official report. Standing where the eleven died, she reads their names aloud. Emotional beat: the case stops being abstract; it becomes a debt.

chapters.title: Voss Closes a Door
chapters.summary: Voss's POV. He eliminates the program's leak investigator — the one man who might have exposed Marek first — and reports upward that Odile will run the harbor route. But he pockets one document himself. Emotional beat: first hairline crack in his obedience.

chapters.title: The Third Government
chapters.summary: Ministerial aide Lena Brandt's POV. In Berlin, she learns her own ministry signed off on the cover-up and that she's been assigned to discredit any leak. She recognizes Odile's name from an old debrief. Emotional beat: institutional loyalty beginning to rot from the inside.

chapters.title: Dead Drop, Live Wire
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. The Brussels handoff with Tomas goes wrong — a second surveillance team, not Voss's, forces them to scatter. Tomas is detained. Odile escapes with half the archive chain of custody intact. Emotional beat: fury and guilt; the cost of moving truth through hostile territory.

chapters.title: Interrogation Room 4
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. Detained without charges, Tomas stalls interrogators by reciting archival regulations verbatim, buying time while a hidden backup uploads. Emotional beat: dignity under pressure; the pen as a weapon.

chapters.title: Marek Makes His Case
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Marek corners her in Vilnius, gun visible, and argues he sold her location to save her — the alternative was Voss's employers cleaning house entirely. He offers her exile and silence. Emotional beat: the theme made flesh — loyalty asking her to bury the truth.

chapters.title: Nine Days Become One
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs converge. The sale accelerates; Voss repositions; Lena leaks the ministry's disinformation plan to Ines. Odile realizes publication must happen tomorrow, inside the press deadline, or never. Emotional beat: breathless compression — every clock striking at once.

chapters.title: The Upload
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. From a rented office above a shuttered print shop, she releases the full archive — logs, payments, names — to forty newsrooms simultaneously. Alarms sound below as Voss enters the building. Emotional beat: terrible calm; the moment anonymity dies on purpose.

chapters.title: Voss and the Man Who Ordered Him
chapters.summary: Confrontation POV alternating Odile/Voss. Trapped on the roof, Odile doesn't run; she shows Voss the order authorizing his own termination once the job closed. He lets her walk down the stairs. Emotional beat: justice outside the law — truth as the only weapon that worked.

chapters.title: Aftermath, Broadcast
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. The story detonates globally; resignations cascade through three governments; Tomas walks free when his detention becomes indefensible. Ines protects Odile's location even from her editors. Emotional beat: vindication shadowed by everything it cost.

chapters.title: Marek's Reckoning
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. She testifies anonymously via video while Marek faces arrest, and he mouths 'thank you' as they take him away — or perhaps 'forgive me.' She visits the eleven families' memorial wall. Emotional beat: accountability without satisfaction; justice is a process, not a moment.

chapters.title: One Name
chapters.summary: Odile's POV, final chapter. Months later, in a small coastal town, she burns three identity kits and keeps one passport: her birth name, Ulyana. She plants a garden where a safe house used to be. Emotional beat: quiet resolution — visibility chosen freely, memory carried openly, the war over.
